rv.q: 'Here We Are' is as experimental as Sondheim throughout his career wanted everything to be.
'Here We Are' is more broadly funny than the films and also more overtly philosophical, with a recurring theme about the gap between appearances and reality—though it doesn't go all that deep.
If it's sometimes a muddled impulse, it's also a humane one.
The resulting evening might not be stranded at square one, but it doesn't satisfactorily cross the finish line, either.
'Here We Are' delights in the flavor of its vapid jet-sets, but ultimately spits them out in a resolution that betrays its own internal logic.
The novelty of attending Sondheim's final musical and experiencing its non-stop zaniness wear off long before 'Here We Are' ends, and the whole thing falls apart.
It's a surrealist puzzle that Sondheim and Ives clearly enjoyed trying to solve — and we'd be hard-pressed not to enjoy it ourselves.

...’Here We Are,’ now having its world premiere at The Shed, watching an inventive, ambitious, brilliantly acted musical without a full score by the master – and with almost every note confined to the mostly jaunty act.
But if Here We Are remains an unfinished work, it still has plenty to offer, especially in Mantello's lovingly realized production...
“Considering that it’s the final musical by the renowned composer-lyricist who died in 2021, Stephen Sondheim’s ‘Here We Are’ was guaranteed to jolt.
Ives and Mantello do heroic work endowing it with coherence and force.
It contains fewer songs than you would expect in a two-and-a-half hour show, but we should take what gems we can get.

Sondheim’s music has a thrillingly familiar sound...but on first listen it seems so seamlessly integrated into Ives’ dialogue that it’s hard to imagine being turned into discrete songs for the bourgeoisie at piano bars… Ives’ adaptation streamlines Buñuel’s films for the stage and adds its own comic flourishes, but it’s faithful enough to the...
It's hard to imagine any staging more perfect than Mantello's, whose masterful comic blocking includes a final image that's somehow both haunting and exhilarating.
'Here We Are' probably did not merit a full-scale, sleek, starry production – but I suppose that it had to be produced posthumously anyway in tribute to Sondheim.
The potential of the story's characters and situations seems rich enough and might well have resulted in memorable music and lyrics.

The production values are dazzling. Joe Mantello’s smart, stylized direction of this stellar ensemble is a joy to behold...Meanwhile, for lovers of Sondheim and musical theater, it is imperative to see this vibrant production of ‘Here We Are’ at The Shed, filled with vitality and creativity.
This was a show that fully grasped these concepts.
Although 'Here We Are' leaves you hungry for completion, it's a slow-crawling nightmare that plink-pla-plink in your consciousness long after you leave the theatre.
